My research studies two sets of decisions that shape economic mobility in Latin America: how smallholder farmers engage with agricultural markets, and how workers build pathways into formal-sector employment. This work comes from 20 years of experience working with Latin Americans: in the US, on the US/Mexico border, in southern Mexico, and in northern Peru. It seeks to influence not only the academy but also policy to improve the lives of people across the region.

## Agricultural value chains

One strand of my work examines the market-access, contracting, and information frictions that determine which smallholders thrive. Southern Mexico offers a setting in which these frictions can be observed and measured: indigenous coffee producers, organized into agricultural cooperatives of varying strength, sell into global value chains that repeatedly break and reform around them. Through [fieldwork](community.html) in Chiapas, I study who joins cooperatives, how membership shapes household welfare, and what happens when those relationships break down. The work below uses a household survey and lab-in-the-field experiment that our team collected and administrative data from the coffee cooperative spanning over 20 years of producer records and geolocated coffee parcels. The work is supported by the [Center for International Food and Agricultural Policy](https://experts.umn.edu/en/organisations/center-for-international-food-and-agricultural-policy) at the University of Minnesota and the [Ralph K Morris Foundation](https://www.ralphkmorrisfoundation.org/).

## Pathways into formal-sector employment

A second strand examines the pathways workers take into formal-sector employment. Three mechanisms matter: government subsidies that shape internal migration out of agriculture, worker referrals that mediate entry into formal jobs, and access to technical education. I work with harmonized Mexican census data from [IPUMS](https://international.ipums.org/international/) and confidential employer-employee data from the [EconLab](https://www.banxico.org.mx/EconLab/inicio) at the Bank of Mexico, and in Peru I study how licensing technical institutes reshaped access to them, using longitudinal data that track students' socio-emotional skills from childhood.

## Catholic Social Teaching

A third thread of my work reflects on economics through the lens of my own Jesuit tradition. As a priest-economist, I engage with how Catholic Social Teaching bears on questions of poverty, development, and economic ethics.
